stem.en: Kabir says: "A and U have two bonds, G and C have three. So G-C is a different kind of thing, and A-U is weak and useless." What is true?

text.en: Both are the same kind of thing: hydrogen-bonded pairs of the same width. G-C holds a little more tightly. A chain rich in G-C is harder to pull apart, and that difference is used, but A-U pairs are real pairs.

feedback.en: Two hydrogen bonds are enough to hold a pair together at body temperature. Water itself is held by hydrogen bonds.
All three are hydrogen bonds between two separate molecules. No shared pair forms. The bases can still be pulled apart.
It matters a bit. Three bonds hold harder than two, and Book IV's next module measures exactly that.

explanation.en: Same kind, different strength. Count the bonds to know how tightly, and check the width to know that both fit the same slot.
